skill.name: connector-googlemail
skill.description: Guides Caffeine AI developers through Gmail OAuth and Gmail API integration using Motoko packages, per-user token storage, callback routes, and refresh-aware email sending.
skill.summary: Build Gmail account connections and send email from Caffeine apps with per-user Google OAuth.
skill.author: caffeinelabs

security_audit.summary: All 255 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown backticks, documented Google and Mops URLs, fixed relative links/imports, ellipses, and Gmail or OIDC terminology. Semantic review found unvalidated RFC 5322 headers and a disconnect flow that deletes local state without revoking Google's refresh token.

remediation.issue: Untrusted address and subject text enters RFC 5322 headers.
remediation.suggestion: Reject CR/LF in recipient and subject values, validate mailbox syntax, and use a MIME builder that safely serializes headers.

remediation.issue: The disconnect endpoint does not revoke Google authorization.
remediation.suggestion: Call Google's token revocation endpoint for the refresh token before deleting local state, and report revocation failures to the user.

content.user_title: Build Gmail Connections for Caffeine Apps
content.value_statement: Gmail integrations require careful OAuth, token storage, and callback handling. This skill provides a complete Motoko and frontend recipe for connecting accounts and sending email.
actual_capabilities: Provides versioned Mops commands for the Gmail client, Google OAuth, and Caffeine authorization packages.
Defines per-user Authorization Code with PKCE flows and caller-keyed token storage.
Supplies Motoko examples for admin credentials, OAuth completion, connection status, and disconnection.
Sends plain-text Gmail messages and refreshes an expired access token once after HTTP 401.
Defines admin settings, callback, connection status, and empty-state requirements for the frontend.
Explains one shared Google OAuth connection for combined Gmail and Calendar applications.
limitations: Targets Caffeine AI applications built with Motoko on the Internet Computer.
Requires Google Cloud configuration, deployed callback origins, and three external Mops packages.
Demonstrates message sending; mailbox reads and other Gmail operations require additional scopes and implementation.
The sample disconnect removes local state but does not revoke the Google refresh token.

use_cases.title: Add Gmail Sending
use_cases.description: Implement authenticated email sending from each user's Gmail account with minimal scopes and automatic token refresh.

use_cases.title: Build OAuth Screens
use_cases.description: Create reachable credential settings and callback routes that preserve OAuth state and wait for actor readiness.

use_cases.title: Combine Google Services
use_cases.description: Share one OAuth connection, credential set, and union scope across Gmail and Google Calendar features.

prompt_templates.title: Create Send-Only Gmail
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a send-only Gmail connector for my Caffeine app. Use the documented Mops versions, per-user PKCE, and the smallest required scopes.

prompt_templates.title: Add OAuth Frontend
prompt_templates.prompt: Add admin Gmail settings and a real /connect/gmail callback route. Show the exact redirect URI and wait for authenticated actor readiness.

prompt_templates.title: Extend Mailbox Access
prompt_templates.prompt: Extend the connector to list Gmail messages. Request gmail.readonly only for reading, preserve non-replicated calls, and retry once after a 401.
prompt_templates.scenario: Add Gmail reading with least privilege.

prompt_templates.title: Unify Gmail and Calendar
prompt_templates.prompt: Create one shared Google OAuth flow for Gmail and Calendar. Use union scopes, one connection map, and separate non-replicated client configurations.

output_examples.input: Build a send-only Gmail connector for signed-in users.
output: Dependencies use the documented Gmail, OAuth, and authorization package versions.
Each user completes a PKCE flow and receives caller-keyed backend token storage.
The send operation uses the Gmail send scope and one refresh attempt after HTTP 401.
The frontend includes reachable settings and callback routes.

output_examples.input: Combine Gmail sending with Google Calendar access.
output: One admin credential set serves both Google services.
One callback exchanges the authorization code for a shared per-user connection.
The consent request contains the union of required Gmail and Calendar scopes.
Each API creates its own non-replicated client configuration from the shared token.

best_practices: Request only the Gmail scopes required by implemented operations.
Keep client secrets and bearer tokens in the canister behind caller and admin checks.
Use one exact callback URI, generate state on the backend, and validate it before token exchange.
anti_patterns: Do not hand-roll Google HTTP requests when the documented OAuth and Gmail packages provide the operation.
Do not return client secrets, access tokens, refresh tokens, or complete connection records to the frontend.
Do not create separate OAuth flows for Gmail and Calendar when both use the same Google account.

faq.question: Which applications does this skill support?
faq.answer: It supports Caffeine AI applications written in Motoko for the Internet Computer.

faq.question: Whose address sends the email?
faq.answer: Messages are sent from the signed-in user's connected Gmail account, not a shared application mailbox.

faq.question: Which scopes are required for sending?
faq.answer: Use openid, email, and gmail.send. Add gmail.readonly only when the application reads mailbox data.

faq.question: Can the frontend access OAuth tokens?
faq.answer: No. The recipe keeps tokens in caller-keyed canister state and returns only status, email address, and authorization URLs.

faq.question: Does disconnect revoke Google access?
faq.answer: No. The sample removes local connection state only. Production applications should revoke the Google refresh token before deletion.

faq.question: How should Gmail and Calendar share OAuth?
faq.answer: Use one credential set, one callback route, union scopes, and one per-user connection shared by both service clients.
